Britain's landlords are getting bigger. A two-tier rental market may follow

On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out.

"The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls.

Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.

The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market — individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.

Lexi Levens received a letter on Christmas Eve 2021 telling her that her family had to move out

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions — be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.

Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

Not everyone is convinced BTR landlords are better, though.

Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" — an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.

"They just look like big, money-grabbing deals," he says.

Clint Stevenson sometimes walks his landlady's dog and does her shopping too

In Cardiff, Grainger, the UK's largest listed BTR developer, is currently offering a fully-furnished studio flat on the 20th floor of The Copper Works in the city centre with views over the bay for £1,265 a month.

It's a lot more than what is currently on offer on Rightmove, a 15 minute walk away from the city centre – a fully-furnished, ground-floor, one-bedroom flat with a garden for £800 a month.

But tenants in The Copper Works have free access to a gym, a cinema room, a roof terrace, and a games room. There's also free WiFi, a concierge service with a helpline, and other amenities. In addition, the studio flat has an EPC B rating as opposed to an EPC C rating for the one-bedroom flat down the road.

"You have to look at what you're getting for your rent," says Helen Gordon, Grainger's chief executive. She says BTR landlords can offer these services because of their scale. As she puts it: "If you run 11,000 homes, you can afford to invest in systems, processes, people, helplines – that sort of thing – that smaller landlords can't."

Gordon strongly pushes back against suggestions that there is a lack of human connection within BTR, noting that tenants are able to speak with staff whenever they need and that the firm regularly organises events for socialising with other tenants to create a sense of community.

It's a pattern across the BTR sector: a higher price point in exchange for what is marketed as high-quality accommodation and a suite of services — some in the sector even refer to 'customers' rather than 'tenants'.

The number of BTR homes has tripled between 2019 and 2025, and while it represents just 3% of the overall rental market at the moment, Gordon believes it could reach "at least 10%" over the next ten years. "And I think it could go higher," she adds.

"If you've got major institutions that include pension funds, financial institutions, and FTSE 250 companies running the stock, it's easier to hold people to account than lots of disparate people, so you can see why it's attractive [to government]."

A 2012 government-commissioned report concluded that more BTR properties could help increase housing supply and drive economic growth as well as providing tenants with more choice and better quality housing. It recommended central government and councils support the development of BTR through favourable planning decisions and releasing public land.

There is a lot of evidence governments and local authorities listened. Local leaders in big cities – London and Manchester, in particular – have partnered with developers to deliver large housing projects involving, in many cases, the release of public land. Kings Cross in London is a prime example of this and current London Mayor Sadiq Khan's push for BTR development near Transport for London (TFL) land, mostly Tube stations, is another example. As part of that, TfL formed a joint venture with Grainger.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, says it's not a matter of looking at one policy, government, or council in particular but more the "policy environment" which has been around since the 2010s.

He points to a series of tax changes, including mortgage interest tax relief changes and higher stamp duty rates for second homes and buy-to-let properties introduced by the Conservatives around 10 years ago, which made the sector less favourable for smaller landlords.

The Renters' Rights Act and more stringent energy efficiency requirements were later introduced. And the last two Budgets have raised taxes on rental income from next year. The tax change applies to individuals who are landlords, not to BTR companies which pay corporation tax, further encouraging professionalisation of the sector.

Yet, while many welcome these changes, others say they are pushing smaller landlords out of the sector. As Cook puts it, there has been more "stick" for small landlords than "carrot" for the BTR sector.

Between 2000 and 2016, a net 2.74 million homes were added to the English rental market in total, according to an analysis of government data by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. In the 10 years since, a net of just 200,000 have. For renters, it is now less likely that your property is owned by a smaller landlord.

Kevin Barber started off with one rental home. He has since grown this portfolio to 40 properties with his business partner but resents what he sees as the clout of the BTR sector. "The big property companies have got so much financial power and influence with the government," he says.

Many experts, landlord groups, and tenant groups agree that building more housing — whether that's rental housing or housing for sale — would help solve many of the issues in the rental sector.

The thinking goes that building more homes for rent, provided people can afford them, would help deal with the supply crunch that can drive up rental costs and force tenants into lower quality properties. And building more homes for sale, provided people can afford them, would remove those from the market who don't want to rent but are forced into it.

Kevin Barber resents what he sees as the clout of the BTR sector.

But whether we will actually see more homes being built is another matter. Savills' Cook says BTR development could slow in future as high interest rates and increased building costs continue to hit developers' bottom line. These same factors are why housebuilders say they are building less.

Cook says the current rate of BTR development won't be enough to meet the demand for rental properties on its own, at least not imminently. In addition, while some BTR developers do build cheaper family homes for rent in the suburbs, the sector is largely still building blocks of flats for wealthier renters living in cities.

This raises the possibility that the UK could end up with a two-tier rental market – what Cook describes as the "haves and the have nots" – where high-earning city-dwelling renters have their pick of rental properties but poorer renters in suburbs struggle to find somewhere to live.

Unless the government steps in, possibly by delivering more housing itself or partnering with developers to do so, it might find any positives gained by the Renters' Rights Act are undone by an increasingly fragmented rental market.

Umushinga w’itegeko rishya rishyiraho Ikigega k’Ibidukikije “Rwanda Green Fund” uteganya ko iki kigega kizagira ububasha bwagutse bwo gukusanya no gushora imari, harimo gukoresha imari ihuriweho no gukurura amafaranga y’abikorera. Ariko uko aya mafaranga azagenzurwa ni kimwe mu bibazo by’ingenzi, kuko umushinga w’itegeko uha Inama y’Ubuyobozi ububasha bukomeye ku ishoramari, imari n’umutungo by’Ikigega.

Umushinga w’itegeko uteganya ko Rwanda Green Fund itazongera kuba cyane cyane ikigega gishingiye ku nkunga nk’uko byari bisanzwe ku kigega cyari gisanzweho kizwi nka FONERWA, ahubwo ikaba urubuga rw’igihugu rwo gukusanya, guhuza, gushora no kongera gukoresha imari igenewe ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe. Harimo no gushyiraho Ishami ry’Ishoramari (Investment Arm) rifite ubuzima gatozi kandi rikora nk’ikigo cyigenga.

Ibi bivuze ko amafaranga azajya acungwa atari inkunga gusa, ahubwo ashobora no kuba imari y’abikorera, imari y’ibigo by’imari n’abashoramari b’inzego zitandukanye, ndetse n’amafaranga ava mu bikorwa by’ishoramari.

Inama y’Ubuyobozi ni yo izaba ifite ububasha bukomeye

Ingingo ya 11 y’umushinga w’itegeko iteganya ko Inama y’Ubuyobozi ya Rwanda Green Fund izaba igizwe nibura n’abantu barindwi, bashyirwaho n’Iteka rya Perezida, barimo Perezida na Visi Perezida. Abayigize bagomba gutoranywa hashingiwe ku bushobozi n’ubumenyi bafite mu byerekeye ibidukikije, kubungabunga ibidukikije, imari cyangwa izindi nzego zijyanye n’inshingano z’Ikigega. Manda yabo ni imyaka itanu ishobora kongerwa inshuro imwe.

Ingingo ya 12 iha iyo Nama ububasha bwo gufata ibyemezo ku buyobozi, abakozi, ishoramari n’umutungo bya Rwanda Green Fund. Ingingo ya 13 na yo ivuga ko Inama y’Ubuyobozi ari rwo rwego rukuru rw’Ikigega kandi ikagira inshingano yo kugenzura no gukurikirana imikorere y’Urwego Nshingwabikorwa.

Ni ukuvuga ko mu buryo bwateganyijwe n’uyu mushinga, icyemezo cya nyuma ku byemezo bikomeye by’ishoramari kitazaba kiri ku Muyobozi Mukuru wenyine, ahubwo kizajya mu rwego rw’Inama y’Ubuyobozi.

Umushinga kandi ushyiraho Urwego Nshingwabikorwa ruyobowe n’Umuyobozi Mukuru. Uyu muyobozi ni we ushinzwe ibikorwa bya buri munsi bya RGF, gushyira mu bikorwa ibyemezo by’Inama y’Ubuyobozi, guhuza gahunda y’ishoramari, no kwita ku micungire y’imari n’umutungo by’Ikigega.

Umuyobozi Mukuru kandi ashyikiriza Inama y’Ubuyobozi imishinga igomba guterwa inkunga kugira ngo iyemeze.

Ariko umushinga w’itegeko uteganya ko Umuyobozi Mukuru yitabira inama z’Inama y’Ubuyobozi ariko ntagire uburenganzira bwo gutora igihe hafatwa ibyemezo. Ndetse ntazitabira inama zifata ibyemezo ku bibazo bimwerekeyeho.

Ibi bishyiraho itandukaniro hagati y’urwego rufata ibyemezo n’urwego rushinzwe kubishyira mu bikorwa.

Mu gihe Rwanda Green Fund izaba ifite ububasha bwo gushora amafaranga mu mishinga itandukanye, ikibazo cy’inyungu bwite na cyo cyahawe umwanya.

Ingingo ya 22 iteganya ko ugize Inama y’Ubuyobozi ufite inyungu bwite, itaziguye cyangwa iziguye, ku ngingo iri gusuzumwa agomba kubimenyesha Inama. Uwo muntu kandi ntiyemerewe kwitabira inama isuzuma iyo ngingo.

Ibi ni ingenzi cyane mu gihe Ikigega kizaba gishobora gukorana n’abashoramari n’ibigo byigenga, kuko amafaranga azaba ashobora gushorwa mu bikorwa bitandukanye by’ubucuruzi.

Umushinga w’itegeko wagura n’inkomoko z’umutungo wa Rwanda Green Fund. Ingingo ya 29 ivuga ko umutungo w’Ikigega ushobora kuva ku ngengo y’imari ya Leta, inkunga za Leta cyangwa abafatanyabikorwa, amafaranga ava muri serivisi zitangwa na RGF, amafaranga ava mu ishoramari, inguzanyo zemewe n’Umuyobozi ufite imari mu nshingano, ndetse n’amafaranga ava mu ihazabu yo mu rwego rw’ubutegetsi, n’izindi nkomoko.

Iri hinduka rije mu gihe Leta ishaka ko Rwanda Green Fund ibasha gukurura imari myinshi y’abikorera no gukoresha uburyo bwinzi nka blended finance, aho imari iva ahantu hatandukanye ihuzwa igashyirwa mu mishinga y’ibidukikije n’ihinduka ry’ibihe.

U Rwanda kandi rwamaze kwagura ibikorwa bya Rwanda Green Fund mu ishoramari, aho Ikigega ubu gitanga inkunga, ishoramari ritaziguye n’andi mahitamo arimo fund of funds (iki twavuga ko ari nk’ikigega cy’ibindi bigega, aho ikigega runaka gishobora gukura amaranga yo gufasha imishinga runaka).

Freddie Potts has started all of Club Brugge's Champions League games

When Liverpool visit Club Brugge on Wednesday they are likely to come up against English midfielder Freddie Potts.

The 23-year-old ended a 16-year association with West Ham in the summer to join the Belgian champions for an undisclosed fee.

And he has started every game, bar one missed through suspension, in all competitions.

After losing to Aston Villa in the Champions League, they have defeated Inter Milan, Lens and PSV.

"It really is a dream because you hear the music and then you see your family in the stands and you remember all the times that you watched Champions League on TV," Potts told BBC Radio 5 Live's Euro Leagues Show.

"You think of all the memories that you make watching it and to be playing in it now is something that every kid dreams of."

Potts' whole life had been based around West Ham. He had been with the club since the age of six and his father Steve, who made 506 appearances for the Hammers, is a first-team coach.

Potts Jr played 28 times for West Ham, with 25 of them coming last season as they were relegated from the Premier League.

He also had loan spells with Wycombe in League One and Portsmouth in the Championship.

"In pre-season my minutes with West Ham were limited, they weren't as much as I wanted and then I spoke with my agent and said 'let's explore options because this season I'm 22, turning 23'," Potts said.

"It's a massive part of my career and I wanted to play. The opportunity of Club Brugge came along with Champions League football, the best club in Belgium and it was an opportunity I couldn't really turn down with how my minutes were going down with West Ham.

"I grew up in the area, going to the stadium watching the games. It was always going to be a tough decision but it was something that I had to do for my career.

"It was an emotional decision because it had to be made quite quickly. It's been the right decision for me and so far I'm enjoying it, I'm loving life here."

Club Brugge won the Belgian title last season and are second, just one point behind leaders Union Saint-Gilloise this campaign.

"It's a physical league," said Potts. "My running and physical stats have been higher than they've ever been. It's a demanding league in that way.

"Club Brugge demands a lot, from winning the ball back and going man for man in the press. And your responsibility off the ball is something that you have to take really seriously."

Freddie Potts on leaving West Ham, life in Belgium and beating Inter Milan

Potts says he has not started to learn French or Flemish and that team talks are done in English, with the side managed by Croat Ivan Leko.

And he revealed he has a lifelong history with the city.

"The whole move itself is funny because we used to visit Brugge when I was a kid," he said.

"We used to come around Christmas, so my family all know the city. And now I'm here they come out as much as they can.

"It's a great city with a lot of culture. It's brilliant. You won't find many places like it."

Next up for the side is the visit of Liverpool this week - with both clubs on nine points after four games.

The Reds are eighth and Club Brugge are ninth in the table.

"Everyone knows Liverpool as a club, the size and the Premier League teams," said Potts, who started for West Ham at home to the Reds last season.

"It's going to be a big game. We're level on points in the Champions League and we've put big performances in this competition and we're hoping that we're going to do the same."

Congolese rebels said they had targeted a warplane preparing to bomb the town of Minembwe

The Democratic Republic of Congo says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.

The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.

Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.

The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.

It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.

Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.

A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."

The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.

Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".

Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.

In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.

He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.

South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".

"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.

The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.

In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.

The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.

Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.

Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.

The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

MN202611_hm2phwyvqq.t:
BBC secret filming shows dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each

When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.

But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.

Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills.

A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.

We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".

The breeder has not responded to our request for comment.

Katie Thornton has spent more than £5,000 on vet bills since buying Ozzy earlier this year

When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking".

But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot.

Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit".

The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence.

In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including:

"Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in

Deteriorating health and welfare of "sad" dogs

Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"

Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"

The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop"

Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her

His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent"

He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first.

Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings).

Dr Caroline Allen, founder of Pet Lighthouse and former RSPCA chief veterinary officer, said she was "surprised and shocked" that the business kept its licence.

A North Yorkshire Council spokesperson said the threshold for revoking a licence "was not considered to have been met on the evidence available".

They added: "We take animal welfare very seriously and investigate concerns brought to our attention.

"Following the veterinary inspection reports, we have continued to work with the licence holder to address the identified concerns and are satisfied that standards have significantly improved, resulting in a higher level of animal welfare at the premises."

The BBC has evidence that Estill continued to sell puppies while claiming on his website and in person that he was five-star rated.

While Estill has since updated his website homepage, he has not updated the metadata, which means when his business is searched for online the five-star claim still appears alongside a link to his site.

There is no official list of licensed breeders and their star ratings, and not all councils publish them, so Katie took his word for it.

"If I would've known he was a one-star breeder, I would've never even gone to the property. I wouldn't have bought a dog off a one-star breeder," she said, adding that she wanted to see Estill's licence revoked.

Kat Durrant's dog Bentley died aged three in 2022 of a heart condition known as dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

Within days of bringing him home from Mikjulora Dobermanns, Kat says Bentley was "really poorly".

"The vet asked me if I had got the dog from a puppy farm because of his condition," she added.

Three years later, Kat had Bentley put to sleep as his weak heart was "giving up" and he was struggling to breathe.

"Bentley suffered his whole life because of everything he'd been through when he was young," she said.

Kat, from Manchester, set up a Facebook group where other people who had bought dogs from Estill could share their experiences.

Including Kat, owners of 17 dogs mentioned in the group said the pets had died before the age of eight, including 10 below the age of four.

Several others claimed their dogs were sick at a young age but survived.

The vet report from December 2025 said Estill was not correctly testing his dogs for DCM despite his website saying that he did test.

The report said the fact that Estill did "nothing" when customers told him about DCM diagnoses was "truly the hallmark of a breeder who does not care about the welfare or improving the breed".

Kat Durrant's dog Bentley died after being diagnosed with a heart condition

Michelle Paton, who lives in Edinburgh, bought her puppy Cruz a week before Katie bought Ozzy.

He had a cough "as soon as he came through the front door" and was diagnosed with pneumonia and possible heart failure a few weeks later.

Michelle was frustrated to discover Kat's Facebook group and felt Estill's licence should have been revoked "years ago".

"If somebody was actually doing their job properly then they would have put an end to him breeding a long time ago," she said.

Caroline Housam, from York, bought her puppy Roxy the day before Katie bought Ozzy.

Roxy started coughing in the car on the journey home.

When Caroline took Roxy to the vet she said she was told there were problems with her glands, and later they found she had a limp and ulcers in her eyes.

She is having ongoing treatment and tests.

"I'm actually angry because I look at my dog and I'm thinking, 'I don't know what lies ahead'," said Caroline.

"When you listen to what other people have said [on Facebook] who have had [dogs] bred from him, her chances of living until two are slim."

Caroline Housam's pup Roxy has ongoing problems with her eyes

To corroborate the claims made, the BBC sent undercover reporters to film at Estill's home, posing as potential puppy buyers.

Estill refused to show us where the puppies and their mother slept.

He said he had "another 15 Dobermanns" in cages in a back room and worried that the neighbours would complain if we went in and they started barking.

He offered to show us the space another day and said he had "nothing to hide".

Reviewing our footage, Allen said this refusal was the "most serious concern" and breached regulations.

She added that the eyes of two of the puppies for sale were " not all normal", citing "a number of abnormalities" such as discoloration and the shape of the eye socket.

Looking at a photo of a male pup taken by the BBC, she said: "That is not a healthy dog."

Estill's licence certificate and star rating were also not visibly on display anywhere, despite government rules saying both should be "clearly and prominently displayed" for customers.

An independent vet told the BBC the breeder should not have sold this puppy as healthy because it has eye "abnormalities"

BBC research has found at least 15 other breeders in England who are also advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than the one they have been given by their local authority.

We checked through a list of 806 breeders with a rating between one and four stars.

Of the 573 breeders rated three-star or below (meaning lower standards), we could not find mention of a rating on their websites, social media pages or in online adverts for puppies in 541 cases.

Of the 32 who did mention a rating, 11 had active adverts claiming to be more highly rated than they really were.

Of the 45 four-star rated breeders to mention a rating, four claimed they were five-star in active adverts.

Drugs running was like 'a paper round' for exploited son, mum says

The man accused of tricking his friends out of £50,000

Ex-workers tell of 'chaotic atmosphere' at new £400m prison

One council confirmed a breeder we enquired about did not have a licence at all, another said they could not find the information we needed, and others took weeks to respond.

The list of breeders was provided by Paws on the Doors, an organisation aiming to collate breeders' star ratings across the country in one place. For each of the breeders whose online claims did not match the Paws on the Doors list, we checked with individual councils to verify the up-to-date rating.

Caroline says she feels "angry" and fears Roxy might not live past two years old

Commenting on the BBC's findings, Paws on the Doors co-founder Leigh Grant said the main reason "the scammers exist" was that central government and local councils had "failed" to properly implement the principles of legislation for breeder licensing from 2018.

He said a lack of support for animal welfare had led to a position where breeders can "falsely claim higher standards, without fear of detection".

Allen said our findings showed puppy breeding was "an absolute wild west" and there should be "countrywide teams of inspectors and vets who are properly trained to understand the legislation".

She said: "It is easy for consumers to be scammed, but unfortunately at the heart of this there are really vulnerable animals and puppies."

Michelle Paton's Dobermann pup Cruz, pictured with her other dog Lupo

Amy Thompson-Copsey, senior public affairs officer at Dogs Trust, said potential puppy owners should "trust your instinct" to avoid falling for "financial scams".

"If something seems off, if you feel red flags, just walk away. You don't know what you could be getting into."

A Defra spokesperson said they were committed to ending "low welfare dog breeding" and were consulting on reforms to protect dogs' health and better inform the public on "which breeders they can trust".

The BBC put all allegations to Michael Estill and his wife Julie Estill, who is the named director of Mikjulora on Companies House, but they did not respond.

I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

How well Muse works really matters to Meta.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging – that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think, regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the the Information Commission's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its CEO, Paul Arnold, added: it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product."

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," says David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he adds, "helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission – but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal. I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its market place, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons", it has said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external

"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it notes.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough. It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

The tech giant is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda – my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alex Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control , external once AI is 1000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

Buttermere has been described as a "fragile ecosystem under pressure"

Tourism, infrastructure challenges and "outdated, undersized and poorly maintained" wastewater systems are contributing to the ecological decline of a popular lake, an environmental group has warned.

Buttermere, in the Lake District, has seen rising nutrient levels in recent years which can lead to excess phosphorus and blankets of algae.

A new report has found farming practices alone "cannot account" for the changes.

West Cumbria Rivers Trust (WCRT), a charity which tracked down the sources of phosphorus for the study, argues "urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed".

The Buttermere Nutrient Investigations Project was commissioned and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) after the lake was last year found to be failing to meet total phosphorus targets.

WCRT said the investigation showed Buttermere - a designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and Special Area of Conservation - was a "fragile ecosystem under pressure".

Buttermere is a naturally nutrient-poor lake, the organisation said, which provides a welcoming environment for sensitive species, such as the Arctic charr cold-water fish.

But algae triggered by excess phosphorus can "choke out these rare habitats and degrade the lake's protected status", WCRT added.

Local wastewater infrastructure was identified as a "key area of concern", the organisation said, while agricultural investigations across major landholdings found no evidence of systemic diffuse pollution or excessive nutrient use, with soil management plans broadly appropriate.

As they are not connected to mains drainage, many properties in the area rely on septic tanks or package treatment plants.

However, WCRT said a number of the 11 septic tank systems identified in the catchment were "undersized, poorly maintained or past their effective lifespan, with several suspected to be discharging directly to surface water, which is not compliant with the regulations".

Although most owners were keen to help the environment, the trust said there was a "widespread lack of awareness" about how the private systems worked and what level of maintenance was needed.

Surveys also revealed just over 40% of visitors had dogs with them and many were walked along sensitive lakeshore paths.

Nutrient fertilisation by the animals "could be significant", it was found.

WCRT CEO Jodie Mills, said: "Our investigations show that water quality in Buttermere is suffering primarily due to private wastewater systems that are undersized, poorly maintained or overwhelmed during peak seasonal surges.

"Many home and business owners simply didn't realise their tanks weren't performing properly.

"This creates a hidden source of pollution, and urgent regulatory action and maintenance guidance are needed to protect this special lake."

In addition to calling for regulation and enforcement, the trust said it would be providing wastewater guidance for homeowners on its website and engaging with the local parish council and the Lake District Visitor Management Group, which includes the National Trust and the Lake District National Park Authority.

Responsibility for the regulation of discharges belongs to the EA.

Peter Miles, the organisation's nature, monitoring and technical manager, said the report provided "valuable information about the sources of excess nutrients" in Buttermere.

He added: "Sources of pollution are often very complex and we urge everyone living or working in Buttermere, and those visiting, to play their part in reducing the amount of pollution entering the lake, from checking their private sewage systems to clearing up after their dogs."

Newly-released bodycam footage shows the moment troops entered a house and detained a Mexican drug lord who had managed to evade capture for years.

The video shows armed personnel entering via a garage and finding Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, also known as 'El Chapo Isidro', who was on the FBI's most wanted list.

Seven suspects were killed in last Friday's operation, as were four members of the Mexican army who were travelling to reinforce security in Guasave, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Isiah Noel-Williams has been remanded in custody

League Two footballer Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged with rape.

Noel-Williams, who plays for League Two side Barnet, has been charged with three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault by penetration, Hertfordshire Police said.

The 23-year-old, of High Oaks, St Albans, was remanded in custody following a hearing at Hatfield Magistrates' Court on Saturday.

In a statement, the club said it was "co-operating fully with authorities" and would determine further action "in due course".

Noel-Williams has also been charged with one count of engaging in sexual communication with a child, and one count of supplying a controlled (Class B) drug, police added.

In a statement, the London club said: "Barnet FC can confirm that first-team player Isiah Noel-Williams has been charged and remanded in custody as part of a police investigation by Hertfordshire Constabulary.

"The club is co-operating fully with the authorities and will determine any further action in due course.

"As this is now a matter for the courts, the club will not be making any further comment."

Noel-Williams, who previously played for Hemel Hempstead Town, Kettering Town, Matlock Town, Harrow Borough and Cheshunt, joined Barnet in June.

A larger section of Rwandan consumers are at a high risk of falling prey to digital scammers according to findings in a survey.

Concerns have emerged over growing identity theft and digital fraud while Rwanda continues its rapid digital transformation.

New findings from TransUnion’s H2 2026 Update to the Top Fraud Trends Report show that 62% of Rwandans surveyed reported being targeted by email, online, phone call or text messaging fraud during a recent three-month period.

Furthermore, in TransUnion’s Q1 2026 Consumer Pulse Study, when asked what consequences beyond accessing credit cards or financial accounts Rwandans were most concerned about, the top answer was someone might use their identity to commit a crime (62%), followed by gaining access to workplace systems (45%).

As more Rwandans use mobile money, online banking, e-commerce websites and digital government services, personal information and account credentials have become increasingly attractive targets for cybercriminals.

Among the 62% who said they were targeted with a digital fraud scheme recently, the most reported scams were:

Vishing through fraudulent phone calls meant to trick people into revealing personal information (30%)

Third-party seller scams on legitimate e-commerce sites (29%)

Vishing being reported as the second most common fraud scheme suggests that fraudsters continue to rely heavily on trusted communication channels and social engineering tactics to deceive consumers.

By creating urgency, impersonating trusted organisations or exploiting consumer trust, criminals are often able to convince victims to share personal information, approve fraudulent transactions or transfer money.

Fraud Increasingly Begins With Trusted Communications

While organisations may have invested heavily in strengthening authentication controls over the past decade, fraudsters have evolved their tactics in response.

Fifty-eight percent of business leaders surveyed by TransUnion globally said they were very or extremely concerned that fraud risk is evolving faster than their organisation’s ability to detect and prevent it.

As fraud becomes more sophisticated, Rwandan consumers are also increasingly alert to the methods criminals use to obtain personal information.

When asked which identity attack methods concern them most, many responded that there was more than one they were worried about:

46% were concerned about viruses or malware

These concerns reflect a growing understanding that fraud often begins long before money is stolen or an account is compromised.

Criminals frequently start by gathering personal information, building trust or harvesting credentials before attempting to impersonate consumers and gain access to accounts.

“Today’s fraud landscape extends far beyond traditional online scams,” said Didier Mutabazi, CEO at TransUnion Rwanda.

“Criminals are increasingly combining stolen identities, compromised credentials and AI-powered deception to target consumers at scale. Artificial intelligence is changing the economics of fraud by enabling criminals to automate activities that historically required significant human effort. From generating convincing content and synthetic identities to personalising attacks and interacting with victims, AI is improving the precision, scale and adaptability of fraud campaigns,” he added.

AI Is Accelerating The Scale And Sophistication Of Fraud

TransUnion identifies AI-enabled adaptive attacks as one of the defining global fraud trends in the H2 2026 Update and notes that 42% of business leaders surveyed globally said the increasing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant to severe pressure on their organisations.

AI is helping criminals increase the effectiveness of fraud schemes at unprecedented speed and scale.

By lowering the cost and effort required to execute sophisticated attacks, it enables fraudsters to exploit legitimate business processes, steal assets and move illicit proceeds more efficiently.

“AI is not creating new fraud, it’s making existing fraud faster, cheaper, more convincing and dramatically more scalable,” added Mutabazi.

“The future fraudster may not be a criminal syndicate with thousands of members. It may be a small, highly automated operation powered by generative AI.”

In Africa Most Suspected Digital Fraud Occurred At Account Login, Financial Services Industry Most Targeted

The report also found that 94% of suspected digital fraud activity among Africa clients in H1 2026 occurred during account login, significantly higher than the global average of 53%.

This highlights the prevalence of credential theft and account takeover attacks and how identity theft can have consequences far beyond financial loss. Stolen personal information can be used to access accounts, impersonate legitimate individuals, apply for services fraudulently and exploit trusted digital systems.

Another finding in the report involving TransUnion’s Africa clients included that the financial services industry recorded the highest suspected digital fraud rate in H1 2026 among industries analysed at 3%, reflecting growing challenges associated with digital banking, mobile money lending and real-time payment services

As digital ecosystems continue to expand, organizations are being encouraged to adopt smarter, risk-based approaches that balance security with customer experience.

“With Rwanda’s digital transformation depending on consumers trusting mobile finance, e-commerce websites and digital public services, identity verification remains essential when an account is opened, but login activity, device changes, account recovery requests and financial transactions often require additional context,” said Mutabazi.

“Linking identity to trusted devices, monitoring behavioural changes and applying real-time risk assessment through a layered approach can help organisations distinguish a genuine customer from a criminal using valid credentials. Security and convenience need to advance together. Stronger identity assurance, device intelligence, behavioural analytics and risk-based authentication can protect customers without introducing unnecessary friction that slows inclusion and adoption,” he added.

Most data cited in this press release is in TransUnion’s H2 2026 Update to its Top Fraud Trends Report: Fraud in the Age of Continuous Trust.

However, some other data cited is drawn from TransUnion commissioned business and consumer surveys, including the Q1 2026 Consumer Pulse Study of 259 Rwandans, as well as insights derived from TransUnion’s proprietary global intelligence network.

Major League Soccer side FC Cincinnati will honour Fiona, a hippo that recently died at the city's zoo, with a tifo display at their match with Nashville SC on Saturday.

Fiona, a social media star since her premature birth at the zoo in 2017, died on Thursday after swallowing a woollen hat that had slipped into her enclosure.

The Ohio side will now raise a banner depicting the nine-year-old semi-acquatic mammal in their post-season MLS Cup encounter with Nashville, who won the Supporters' Shield for being the highest-placed team in the league campaign.

Cincinnati said Fiona was a "beloved hippo who became a symbol of Cincinnati and captured hearts around the world".

The tifo will be produced by fan group The Forge Cincy, who painted the display on Sunday in a garage next to Cincinnati's TQL Stadium.

The club will also make a donation in Fiona's memory for every fan in attendance to the Cincinnati Zoo and Botanical Garden.

Mark Robins (Stoke City), Cesar Peixoto (Wolves), Chris Davies (Birmingham City) and James Morrison (West Bromwich Albion) all have cause to feel content

It is beginning to look a lot like Christmas for followers of Midlands football.

Granted, it is actually only November, but with more than a third of the 2026-27 Championship season gone, already the table is taking on an increasingly familiar weekly look in terms of the primary promotion contenders.

There has been many a year when there have been early-season stirrings in the Midlands, only for the momentum to fade.

But Coventry City proved it can be done after 25 years away from the Premier League. And now Stoke City, Wolves, Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion are all in contention to join both the Sky Blues and Aston Villa in the top flight.

Stoke in second, Wolves third, Blues fourth and Albion fifth makes for both a heartening, yet surprising sight, with only Middlesbrough in front of them.

It is only six months since Wolves were relegated and, for all the summer discontent at Molineux and doubts among disillusioned fans about their worthiness as serious candidates, the fact is they are very much in the mix.

But, while most people at Molineux can now at least contemplate a quick return, for their local rivals the parachute payments have long since expired.

Blues have been away the longest, their 15-year absence from the top flight having even included a one-season return to the third tier and back.

But, given their extensive American backing, the club have ambitions to be serious contenders - and the only surprise was that it took so long to find their feet.

For Stoke and Albion to be up there was not necessarily forecast, but it has made for all the more happy motoring for the BBC correspondents who cover the quartet of clubs on a regular basis.

BBC Sport asked reporters from BBC Stoke & Staffordshire and BBC West Midlands Sport for their analysis of the season so far and what lies in store for each club...

Mark Elliott, BBC Radio Stoke commentator

Mark Robins has spoken a lot about evolution and incremental gains in his time as Stoke City manager, but it's hard to escape the feeling that there's been a full-blown revolution over the past three months.

Stoke began the season with three defeats, a manager under pressure and the impending loss of their most productive player in Sorba Thomas - but a change in formation, an excellent summer transfer window and an unbelievable run of form has quietened all dissenting voices.

Thirty two out of a possible 39 points from 13 games since the window closed is a brilliant record - but Stoke are maybe still short of truly turning the hopefully optimistic among their fans into true believers.

Most of that is a hangover from last season's promising start eventually falling apart, but there are substantial differences.

The squad has more quality and depth, a more ambitious way of playing and the less quantifiable qualities of tenacity and resilience and a mental strength that, coupled with defensive solidity, has allowed them to find multiple ways to win close games.

Luke Graham, Ethan Galbraith, Jack McGlynn and Ben Johnson have been their most eye-catching summer acquisitions but several who struggled last season, Eric Bocat first among them, have found success too.

The next step is to create more chances and score more goals, whilst maintaining anything close to their current return of points per game.

Even the most hardened pessimists will then maybe see a play-off place as a realistic aim for 2027.

By Mike Taylor, BBC Radio WM commentator

Only a point behind, and with the feeling they have not played to their full ability very often yet - not very often for 90 consecutive minutes, certainly - Wolves are not badly placed.

Their supporters can be hard taskmasters at the moment, and can hardly be blamed for that in view of the mess of recent seasons and the big promises made of going full-tilt to get straight back up.

For all the understandable misgivings, though, there is a clear path towards achieving it.

Reaching the end of that path may require some judicious spending in January to tidy up a squad that still looks imbalanced, with a surfeit of players in some areas and a shortage in others.

Personal surges in form, from Fer Lopez early in the season to Adam Armstrong more recently, have covered up the gaps and reminded everyone that this squad is not short of class at this level.

Cesar Peixoto, new to England, has handled a delicate situation in a tumultuous league with quiet confidence.

He will have to complete the job in May before he can claim credit more widely, but appears to realise the power he can harness if, like a certain Portuguese predecessor, he can unify all the forces around the club to point in the same direction.

For all of the outside noise about the future of Chris Davies, the Birmingham City board have steadfastly backed their man. Now that decision is paying dividends.

Thanks to that rarely tried footballing trait of continuity, they spent the international break sitting at the top of a very congested Championship table.

But Saturday's 1-0 loss against 10-man Stoke was a reminder of just how tight the division is.

The reboot of the squad started in earnest in January, when the future for Davies was at its wobbliest.

The £18m-plus combined investment in Colombian midfielder Jhon Solis, Danish striker August Priske and Spanish winger Carlos Vicente gave them a chance to bed in to English football over the second half of this season, before kicking on this time around.

Priske, at 22, has a high ceiling. His six Championship goals this season has come with improved physicality and increased confidence.

The industry and physique of Solis have stabilised Blues midfield, while Vicente is one of four options on the wing following the loan addition of Liam Millar.

Davies himself has learned from his first Championship season. His team are now versatile, more able to move the ball forward quickly, no longer wedded to possession at all costs.

Defensively too there is a greater resilience and a visible hunger to succeed.

Whether they are serious contenders for automatic promotion remains to be seen, but they have the ingredients to retain a top six spot over the full 46-game course."

James Morrison's mind was at ease over this international break following Albion's 3-0 win over Millwall.

He is refusing to reveal any pre-season expectations, but looking at the Championship table makes for satisfying reading.

Certainly externally, nobody expected the Baggies to be fifth - just one point off the automatic promotion places - a third into this campaign.

Morrison has now racked up 51 points from 30 league games in charge. That includes his three interim spells, although the second was a single game as head coach in the FA Cup in January against their next opponents, Swansea City - in between the dismal reigns of Ryan Mason and Eric Ramsay.

It is wild to think of the difference Morrison and his excellent coaching staff have made in 2026.

Albion were heading in the direction of League One when the key were handed to the club legend, who'd been in the back seat the entire time.

A 10-game unbeaten run steered them to safety, and he even had to navigate a points deduction from the EFL for a breach of financial rules.

The club is in a much better place on and off the field, with Mozza now firmly at the wheel.

The upcoming January transfer window could play a big part in determining whether they continue on this positive path, but Baggies fans are at least enjoying the ride again.

Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Derry has paused routine appointments for the second time in a week

A GP surgery has suspended all routine appointments due to what it calls a "tsunami" of demand.

It is the second time in a week that Aberfoyle Medical Practice in Londonderry has told patients that it is not offering routine appointments - either in person or online.

Dr Donna Mace, who is a partner at the practice and also a member of the Northern Ireland General Practitioners' Committee, said the practice was currently dealing with unprecedented demand.

In real terms, that means their doctors are seeing around 60 patients a day, which she said, "is not safe".

Dr Mace says the decision was taken due to concerns about patient safety

BBC News NI has contacted the Department of Health (DoH).

"Aberfoyle is one of the biggest practices in Derry and we are really fortunate in that we have 11 doctors, social workers, physios, mental health practitioners and counsellors but unfortunately the last few weeks have just not been manageable at all," the doctor told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today programme.

"Every single day the appointments have been filled up, so much so, that every on-call doctor is dealing with 60 patients per day.

She said the GPs were feeling "rushed" that there is another 59 patients waiting.

"In my on-call, that is dealing with emergency mental health patients, patients in palliative care and very ill children and it was just not manageable.

"I am a partner at the practice and we employ four salaried doctors and there was a risk of losing those doctors, if we lost them due to stress or resignation because they couldn't cope - they were very upset - that would mean we would lose 100 appointments so we had to manage the risk."

"They couldn't go on and there was a total crisis".

The doctor said the decision was taken due to concerns about patient safety.

"It was not manageable and it was not safe, no patient is going to appreciate if we miss something because we have less than the usual 10 minutes with them," she said.

"We should not have a situation that we felt we could not manage our patients to the best of our ability.

"We can only deal with urgents [appointments] and we do sincerely apologise for that but we are still providing a service and a very high level of service."

In October, they saw more then 4,000 patients face-to-face, handled 1,500 telephone consultations and dealt with nearly 9,000 prescription issues.

The practice would review the situation on a "day-to-day basis" to determine when it could reopen routine appointments.

"This is like a tsunami every day," she said.

A review into the health board found, in some areas, targets and money "have a greater priority... than the quality and safety of care"

Wales' largest health board is still failing, with "fundamental weaknesses" in governance and management, a new report says.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has been in special measures for nine years in total, with the latest period starting in 2023.

A review of its leadership published on Tuesday found, in some parts, targets and money "have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care".

Committed staff and ability to deliver some strong local services were highlighted.

The review did not suggest splitting up the health board, but Wales' health minister said the findings were "unacceptable" and BCUHB "does not function as a single coherent organisation".

The review was commissioned by the Welsh government in the summer, after it gave Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUHB) a "final chance" to improve after it had spent nearly half of its existence in special measures.

It concluded that senior leadership is "immature and ineffective", with weak senior management putting the quality of patient care at risk.

The report said: "Many areas reported a culture where targets and financial matters have a greater priority for senior management than the quality and safety of care.

"Fear of speaking up was described often… staff did not believe that raising a concern would result in corrective action.

"Despite this, the panel witnessed many teams striving to deliver the very best care they could for patients. "

The health board's chief executive, Carol Shillabeer, previously announced she would be leaving in the new year to take up an NHS role in England.

Her departure follows a string of other senior leaders who have left the organisation in recent months, including the chief operating officer and executive director of finance.

The report also said that bureaucracy and slow decision-making led to a "loss of local ownership" and staff feeling frustrated.

The reviewers wrote: "Staff and leaders described decisions moving through multiple layers of approval, authority becoming concentrated at senior levels and operational leaders lacking sufficient autonomy to act.

"A phrase used in a focus group characterised the resulting complexity as 'Betsi spaghetti'."

However, the review concluded the health board could still be improved without being broken up into smaller organisations - an option previously discussed by ministers.

It said staff were "loyal and committed", and there were "strong local services" and "significant clinical expertise across north Wales".

Health Minister Mabon ap Gwynfor, said "these failings are utterly unacceptable".

"I also share the understandable frustrations of staff and patients alike in north Wales at the lack of progress in delivering and embedding improvements to services and standards of care," he said.

"The report identifies that the health board does not currently demonstrate the organisational conditions required to deliver and sustain reliable improvement.

"It does not function as a single coherent organisation and board governance is immature, impacting on the health board's capability to discharge its accountabilities adequately."

Ap Gwynfor is due to make a statement in the Senedd addressing the report on Tuesday afternoon.

A team of experts is being sent in to help at NHS Grampian after a critical report

A recurring theme in the debate over the problems at NHS Grampian has been concern at a revolving door of senior managers in Scotland's NHS.

A damning report published earlier this month found that failures to learn from mistakes in Grampian had caused "repeated and avoidable harm" to patients.

Health Secretary Angela Constance has now sent in a team of four expert leaders to help drive urgent change by providing "external challenge, scrutiny and practical support".

But three of them previously held senior positions at other boards that also faced serious criticism.

Patient safety commissioner Karen Titchener has voiced "reservations" about those being asked to improve safety in one board when so many other boards had their own problems to solve.

And the lawyer representing a whistleblower who highlighted serious concerns at NHS Grampian has compared the situation in Scotland to "shuffling of deckchairs on the sinking Titanic".

Eyebrows have been raised about names on the health secretary's team of hand-picked experts who are being sent in to help with NHS Grampian's turnaround.

It is being led by Jim Crombie, deputy chief executive of NHS Lothian.

In 2018, as interim chief executive, he was forced to apologise after an independent investigation found a culture of "bullying and harassment" at the board.

Crombie also apologised for failings in 2024 after a whistleblowing report found mothers and babies had come to harm in the maternity unit at Edinburgh Royal Infirmary because of staff shortages and a toxic workplace culture.

Dr Chris Deighan, a former medical director at NHS Lanarkshire, is also on the team.

He was criticised recently by lawyers for the Scottish Hospitals Inquiry for being an unhelpful witness after he gave evidence on his role in the infection scandal at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Glasgow while he was at NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde.

A third rescue team member, Dr Pamela Johnston, was previously executive medical director at NHS Tayside.

In 2023, she apologised to patients after a review found senior managers at Ninewells Hospital had failed to adequately supervise disgraced neurosurgeon Sam Eljamel , despite a rising number of complaints.

The health secretary has said these external troubleshooters will work with NHS Grampian to turn things around.

She has given them six weeks, and has also made two appointments to the board.

Meanwhile, Constance is sticking by Grampian chief executive Laura Skaife-Knight to get the job done - even though Skaife-Knight herself was found to have misled HIS over the way the death of a patient was investigated.

There are also questions about the performance of former bosses at NHS Grampian, with HIS referring to "long-standing" issues with culture and leadership in that executive team.

At the helm from 2020 to 2023 was Caroline Hiscox, who is now NHS Lothian chief executive - and being tipped to head one of two new super health authorities that would be formed if the government pushes forward with reforms to merge the mainland boards.

She was running NHS Grampian in 2022, at the time of a review into 19 avoidable patient deaths in surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary, which was not made public.

Surgeon Dr Mohammed Habib, who leaked the report last week, said he was risking his job to speak out because he believed senior managers had tried to cover up what was going on.

Dr Mohammed Habib spoke out at a press conference last week

His lawyer Aamer Anwar, a long-time ally of patient safety campaigners, says the current board and chief executive of NHS Grampian should go.

Anwar says there seems to be a permanent crisis in the NHS in Scotland, and people seem to have to accepted a "shuffling of deckchairs on the sinking Titanic, where you have one individual, who hasn't done a good job in one place, is then shuffled off to another place.

"They're all sitting on six-figure salaries so I don't expect the public to have any sympathy for their situation.

"They are just moved around and around in a very small circle, and everybody knows each other, so that causes concern."

On Tuesday, the health secretary is set to announce a review into how concerns over the surgical mortality rate at NHS Grampian were handled by the NHS and by the Scottish government.

Labour MP Dr Zubir Ahmed, who worked in Scotland for the majority of his career as a surgeon, said this must look at the relationship between politicians and senior NHS management.

In an interview with Radio Scotland Breakfast , he said: "It doesn't sit right with me that in NHS Scotland we don't get much of a turnover of senior managers, they move from one place to the next."

Dr Ahmed said getting "the right people in the right jobs" was very important.

Former SNP MSP Alex Neil, who served as health secretary between 2012 and 2014, said there was "too much of the same people doing a job swap almost on a rotational basis" within the NHS.

"I think we need to bring in fresh blood from outside - either outside the health service in terms of management, or outside the country."

Health Secretary Angela Constance is set to announce a review

We asked the Scottish government about these concerns and about the choice of experts sent in to help with improvements at NHS Grampian.

In response, a spokesperson stressed that leadership and accountability for NHS Grampian rested with the chief executive and the health board.

"This is not a leadership team," they said.

"This is an intervention support team which is providing broad external support in organisational and operational recovery, clinical governance, patient safety and performance to support NHS Grampian's improvement. It will not be making decisions.

"The health secretary has been clear she welcomes the involvement of the patient safety commissioner in scrutinising the progress NHS Grampian must make, and we understand she is due to visit Grampian this week."

Constance has decided that the situation at NHS Grampian does not meet the "exceptional circumstances" needed for direct ministerial intervention in the running of the board.

Such a step - known as stage five in the government's escalation framework - has only ever been used once, in Tayside in 2018.

Instead, Grampian will remain at stage four, where it has been since May 2025 due to issues around finances, leadership and governance.

NHS Ayrshire and Arran is also at stage four for financial management, governance and leadership.

That means external support is being provided by a government-appointed "assurance board" at senior levels because the health board leadership has been unable to deliver improvements.

The NHS boards in Borders, Dumfries and Galloway, Highland, Lothian, Orkney and Tayside are all at stage three for different reasons.

This means tailored support and scrutiny is provided by the government because of "risks materialising".

The rest are at level two, with increased monitoring by central government - but none are at stage one, where they would be delivering in line with expectations.

In total, that means eight of the 14 regional health boards in Scotland have some level of government direct intervention at level three or above.

Ni igitero gikurikiye ikindi cikekwa ko cagabwe n'amadrone ya Ukraine ku bwato bw'Uburusiya butwara imizigo mu Kigobe ca Finlande mu mpera z'indwi iheze. Kremlin ( ibiro vy'umukuru w'igihugu c'Uburusiya) yavuze ko ico cari igitero c'iterabwoba.

Imbere y'aho, amadrone ya Ukraine yari yarashe ikigo c'igitoro c'Uburusiya kiri ahitwa Ust-Luga ku nkengera z'Ikiyaga ca Baltique.

Bimwe mu bitero bikomeye cane vya Ukraine bikorwa n'izo ndege, ivyo Zelensky akunda kwita "ibihano bishika kure", vyashitse no ku bibanza biri kure cane y'imbibe za Ukraine n'Uburusiya, mbere no hagati muri Siberia.

Kimwe muri ibi ni ico bise Operation Spider's Web co mu mwaka uheze, carimwo ikamyo yahinduwe mu buryo bwihariye yageze hafi y'ikibuga c'indege z'intambara zirekura ibibombe vya nikleyeri vy'Uburusiya maze irekura amadrone menshi yikoreye ibiturika, yonona canke asambura indege nyinshi z'agaciro kanini.
