Thomas Waites, 22, was found dead hours after celebrating his birthday with friends

A father whose son died by suicide on the day after his 22nd birthday has called for more education on how men and boys can seek help during a mental health crisis.

Seamus Waites said there was "no warning sign whatsoever" before his son Thomas took his own life in May 2016, just hours after he went out to celebrate with friends.

Waites, who has since become a grief counsellor, said when men reach crisis point they "do not understand the emotions that they're feeling, they become totally overwhelmed and don't know where to go".

Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men and boys aged under 50 in Northern Ireland - of the 262 people who took their own lives last year, 203 were male.

This article contains details which some readers may find distressing.

Thomas Waites was a talented young athlete from Magherafelt, County Londonderry, who had represented Ireland in amateur boxing and had a promising career outside the ring ahead of him.

"He had just landed himself a great job, he had bought the car he had always wanted," his father recalled, adding that "from the outside" nothing appeared to be wrong.

Waites went to the gym with his son on the morning of his birthday and said "everything was normal" when Thomas went out that night to celebrate.

The following day, when Thomas did not return home for a barbeque organised in his honour, his father went to check on him at a friend's house.

It was believed Thomas was upstairs listening to music, but when Seamus Waites went into the bedroom, he discovered his son's body.

"You can imagine the shock that it had on us," he said, adding that moment changed his family's lives forever.

Thomas had spent time with his father on the day before his death

Thomas had no known contact with mental health services and even now, a decade on, his family still does not have a full explanation for his death.

"Anybody who takes their own life is in intolerable pain," his father said.

"I think that there needs to be more education around how men cope and how men can reach out."

Waites, who experienced his own mental health struggles after his son's death, now works with an organisation which helps families bereaved by suicide.

"There is an awful stigma about men and how we regulate our emotions," he told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme .

"We are brought up in such a way where we, our families, prepare us to be mentally strong, to be the person that everybody else leans on."

He added the "stigma and shame" associated with not living up to that role meant some men find it difficult to reach out for help when they are in crisis.

On Tuesday night, he will join about 130 families in Ballymena, County Antrim, for a Ceremony of Lights event where their loved ones will be remembered.

Although suicide figures fluctuate each year, the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (Nisra) , external monitors trends by tracking the average every three years.

This method of calculation shows an increasing pattern, with suicides rising by a quarter in less than a decade.

In 2017, the average number of registered suicides stood at just over 204 deaths per year (over the three-year reporting period).

By last year, that number had risen to average of almost 258 deaths per year.

The annual suicide figure for 2025, disregarding averages, stood at a total of 262 deaths, 77.5% of which were men and boys.

Mental Health Champion, Prof Siobhan O'Neill, described the latest figures as deeply concerning.

"Suicide loss is absolutely devastating," she told Good Morning Ulster.

"It changes people's lives forever in a way that's very different to any other sort of bereavement or grief."

O'Neill said not enough was being done address the issue and that patients must be able to access immediate help from "the first time" they report suicidal thoughts.

"Sadly, we can see now when we look at those three-year rolling averages, that we're seeing a rise in Northern Ireland.

"And that's different from the other UK regions and the Republic of Ireland where they're seeing either a flat line or a trend towards a decrease in suicides."

O'Neill said mental health services are underfunded per capita in Northern Ireland compared to England and the Republic of Ireland.

She added authorities must examine what is "driving" the rise in Northern Ireland, arguing there has been a failure to tackle poverty, which is linked high suicide rates.

Pointing to Nisra's figures, she said that nearly a "third of those deaths are in deprived areas".

Thomas Waites was talented amateur boxer who represented Ireland

Waites said people bereaved by suicide are also at higher risk of a mental ill health and it helps to have someone to "navigate you through" those feelings.

"The pain is indescribable and I basically watched my family go through the most tormented emotional feelings that I've ever seen a human being going through."

He said that his initial concern after his son's death was how he was going to support his family.

"I very much took it upon my own shoulders to do that, but at the same time, I was grieving as well."

Waites, originally from London, explained that about a year had passed after his son's death when he "crashed" emotionally.

"At one stage I actually thought that I was losing my mind," he recalled.

"My wife actually turned around and said to me: 'You need help'."

Having benefited from counselling, Waites now works with the Bereaved by Suicide service which is run by the Northern Health Trust.

It provides one-to-one counselling in Ballymena, Cookstown and Coleraine and group sessions led by trained counsellors who have lost loved ones to suicide.

"I didn't realise that there was help out there," he said, adding it was important to raise awareness of such services.

Waites said although his life will never be the same, he wanted to use his "lived experience" to ease the grief of others and help them "learn to live alongside it".

Dowden has been open about her own cancer journey, including her experience with chemotherapy, surgery and egg retrieval

Strictly Come Dancing's Amy Dowden says the upcoming documentary from Catherine, the Princess of Wales, about her cancer journey will help many people, including herself, "not feel so alone".

Dowden praised the documentary and said it confirmed how "anyone can be dealt the devastating blow of a cancer diagnosis".

Dowden, Strictly's first Welsh professional dancer, was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer at 32 and has undergone chemotherapy and two mastectomies .

Catherine's BBC documentary, Heal, will reveal how cancer has impacted her outlook on life, as well as the people, places and experiences that have helped her.

Dowden told ITV's Lorraine she believed the documentary would be "quite raw" and emotional, but "so important" in showing the "truth and effects of cancer".

The dancer said she had a lot of admiration for the princess, adding: "Thank you Princess Catherine for doing this."

Prince William nand Catherine had an official visit to India this month, their first overseas trip together since her cancer treatment

In the trailer for her documentary, Catherine is candid about life-altering effect of the disease, saying: "Cancer does change you."

"It changes your body, it changes you physically... but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you."

Dowden has previously echoed this feeling, saying that after a diagnosis, "in a click of the fingers, your life changes".

"You have everything stripped away from you," she said.

Heal will follow Catherine as she does the National Three Peaks challenge, which involves climbing the highest mountains in England, Scotland, and Wales within 24 hours.

Catherine completed the challenge in June to raise funds for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, the hospital where she underwent treatment, and to "explore life beyond diagnosis".

When the princess revealed she had cancer, Dowden shared her sympathy on Instagram.

Since her own diagnosis in 2023, the dancer has shared her experience of breast cancer online and in the BBC documentary Strictly Amy: Cancer and Me.

She said her decision to let a camera crew film her cancer journey was scary, but she felt a duty to raise awareness.

"I felt straight away, well maybe I could make a difference."

Like Catherine, Dowden's cancer is in remission, and she has been performing in the current series of Strictly.

"It is often through pain that we realise there is a greater beauty that lies beyond that," Catherine says in her new documentary

In Heal, Catherine will discuss how the diagnosis made her "confront her own vulnerabilities".

"When you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite," she shared in a clip from the documentary .

The princess first revealed her diagnosis of cancer in March 2024 and announced she was in remission in January 2025, after chemotherapy.

She has since begun a return to royal duties.

However, she has said she wants to dispel the idea that people can immediately return to how they felt before illness.

Heal will be shown on BBC iPlayer from 12:00 GMT and BBC One at 18:40 GMT on 29 November.

Manchester United defender Ayden Heaven is open to a loan move in January amid concerns over his game time as his side battles in the Premier League relegation zone.

The 20-year-old centre-back is concerned about what United's current situation means for his development, after new manager Mauricio Pochettino left him as an unused substitute in Sunday's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool .

Now on his third manager in 21 months since joining from Arsenal in February 2025, Heaven accepts Pochettino may prefer more experienced options as United attempt to avoid a shock relegation.

The club have also been heavily linked with signing a centre-back in the coming January window, with targets said to include Fulham 's Calvin Bassey.

However, the Cottagers regard Bassey as an important player and would not encourage any interest.

Fulham and Barcelona are among the clubs to have expressed an interest in Heaven, with both having tried to sign him when he decided to leave Arsenal .

The England U20s defender's preference is believed to be a loan move, though he would also entertain permanent offers.

At United he has largely been used as a back-up option and, after enjoying a run in the team under former manager Ruben Amorim, he lost his place under Michael Carrick. He returned to the side only after an injury crisis hit the club last season.

Heaven is also capable of playing at left-back and in midfield, but does not expect to be trusted as a regular starter amid the instability at Old Trafford, with the club 19th in the league.

He is under contract until 2029 in a deal that includes an option for an extra year.

Papa Francis yavuze ko mu buzima bwiwe yabonye shetani incuro zitatu, kandi ko yabonye n'"amarembo y'i kuzimu", nk'uko bigaragara mu gitabu ku vyo yabona canke yacamwo mu buzima bwiwe bwa buri musi.

Muri ico gitabu casohowe ku wa kabiri, harimwo ivyanditswe mu mwaka wa 2021 bivuga ko uwo Mwungere, atakiriho, yabonye shetani incuro zitatu: rimwe ari mu modoka, irindi ari "mu kibanza gitaramutse abaririmvyi baririmbiramwo [mw'isengero]", irya gatatu ari mu nama yagiranye n'abategetsi b'i Vatikano.

Yibuka ivyo yabonye, Papa Francis yanditse ati: "Sinshobora kwibagira urujwi rwayo [shetani] runini kandi rumeze nk'urusaraye."

Muri ico gitabu, canditswe hagati ya 1992 na 2024, agaragaza kandi ko yicuza urugendo yagiriye muri Chili mu 2018, aho yaneguwe ko yari yashingiye inkigi umusenyeri yagirizwa guhishira ihohotera rishingiye ku gitsina ryakozwe n'umupadiri.

Francis, yayoboye Ekleziya Katolika imyaka 12 gushika apfuye mu 2025, yahavuye asaba imbabazi, aca ahamagara abasenyeri b'ico gihugu kuza i Roma, aho bose bemeye gutanga imihoho.

Mu vyo yanditse mu 2021, Papa Francis yagize ati: "Ndashavujwe cane n'ivyabaye muri Chili."

"Vyangoye kwemera ivyabaye muri Chili; sinibaza ko ibintu vyari bikomeye ukuraho."

Ku bijanye n'ivyo yabonye, ivyo Papa Francis afata nk'uguhura na shetani, yavuze ko atoshobora kwibagira amaso "ateye ubwoba" ya shetani.

Avuga ku ncuro ya kabiri yemeza ko yabonye shetani, yanditse ati: "Yarandavye n'amaso asa n'ayariko yakamwo umuriro... yari akaze kurusha ayo nabonye ubwa mbere. Yasa n'urubeya rw'umuriro."

Yavuze ko ivyo vyabereye imbere mw'isengero rito (chepelle) ry'Abakarumeri, igihe yari arongoye diyoseze ya Buenos Aires muri Argentine.

Yavuze ko shetani yamukurikiye no mu ngendo ziwe, harimwo urwo yagiriye muri Chili igihe havugwa cane umusenyeri yagirizwa guhishira ihohotera rishingiye ku gitsina, hamwe no mu nama yagiranye n'abandi haciye imisi mike agarutse i Roma.

Yanditse ati: "Narabonye shetani, ndumva n'ijwi ryiwe, ryumvikana nk'iry'umuntu yishimiye intsinzi kandi afise ububasha ku bintu vyose."

Yongeyeko ati: "Umukama yarampaye akaryo ko kwikura muri ivyo twahuye."

Uwo mupapa atakiriho yavuze kandi ko, muri Ruheshi (6) 2018, igihe yariko yitegurira kuja kuryama, "yabonye amarembo y'i kuzimu".

Yavuze ati: "Nararavye akanya gato, vyaranteye ubwoba", yongerako ko "yafashe ishapure nk'ikirwanisho".

Yanditse ati: "Birateye akaga kwegera amarembo y'i kuzimu, kuko hashobora gusohoka imbeya z'umuriro zikaguturira."

Karidinali Victor Fernandez, arongoye urwego rwa Vatikano rujejwe inyigisho z'ukwemera akaba kandi n'umugenzi wa Papa Francis, ni we yatunganyije ivyo bitabu.

Ni vyo bitabu vya mbere vy'ivyo umupapa yagiye aracamwo mu buzima bwiwe bwa buri musi bisohowe ku mugaragaro kuva mu myaka ya 1960.

Papa Francis yatorewe kuba Umwungere wa Ekleziya mu 2013, apfa muri Ndamukiza (4) 2025 afise imyaka 88.

Wirtz moved from Bayer Leverkusen to Liverpool for £116m in 2025

Florian Wirtz says he is enjoying his best form yet at Liverpool and benefiting from Andoni Iraola's confidence and Jurgen Klopp's advice.

Wirtz, 23, scored in Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United on Sunday and has three goals and six assists this season.

The Germany midfielder made the £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer of 2025 and after failing to make his mark in his first campaign in England, is beginning to showcase his quality for Iraola's side.

Speaking in Belgium before Liverpool 's Champions League game against Club Brugge, Wirtz said: "I can't really say that I've changed that much.

"I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."

He also said he has been picking the brains of Germany manager Klopp, the former Liverpool boss, while on international duty.

"He tells me all the time that he loved his time here, the people love him here and tries to give me some advice to get successful over here as he has shown how it is done," Wirtz said.

"He can give me some good advice. It's always small things. More private things.

"But he is speaking good about the club, the region, the people, and that helps to hear someone who has experienced it for a long time."

On the influence of Iraola, who replaced Arne Slot as Liverpool head coach in the summer, Wirtz added: "He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football, and I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I'm really happy about that.

"I'm just trying to give him back what he gives me."

Liverpool have nine points from their four Champions League games, having won their first three before losing to Fenerbahce in Istanbul this month.

Cody Gakpo and Ryan Gravenberch are both absent from the travelling squad with injuries, with Iraola confirming that Gakpo will be out for the Merseyside derby this weekend, while adding that it is "difficult to say" for Gravenberch.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Shares in Nvidia dipped on Tuesday as US politicans questioned President Donald Trump's role in the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang was handed back his job at the AI microchip maker on Monday less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

Trump has said he played a big role in the 63-year-old's reinstatment, which has led to questions and backlash from US lawmakers.

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the annoucement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price was down almost 8% on Tuesday, but remained well above the level it closed at on Friday, before Huang's shock return was revealed.

However, Nvidia was not the only semiconductor chip company to experience share price declines on Tuesday, with rival AMD down more than 10%.

Broadcom and Marvell Technology shares were also lower, suggesting that investors were continuing to weigh up concerns over potential regulation by newly-elected Democrats, as well as the central question as to whether the huge amounts being invested in AI will pay off.

Nvidia's share price for example, is down almost 30% over the past six months and had been on the decline before the scandal involving its co-founder emerged earlier this month.

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn on its original position. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang.

"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump told CNBC. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."

There has been bipartisan political anger over Huang's reinstatement.

Republican representative Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang", while Republican senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic representative Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions", and Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

The US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

A group of South Africans returned from the war in Ukraine earlier this year

A Zimbabwean national has been convicted by a court in South Africa of planning to go to fight in Ukraine.

The country has strict laws which restrict unauthorised involvement in overseas wars.

Twenty-four-year-old Wesley Sothole, who pleaded guilty, was handed a five-year suspended prison sentence and was ordered to be deported from South Africa.

He is one of five Zimbabweans who were arrested at OR Tambo Airport in Johannesburg on 8 November. South African prosecutors have not confirmed which side the Zimbabweans allegedly intended to fight for.

Sothole's four co-accused have yet to enter pleas and are due to return to the Kempton Park Magistrates' Court on 1 December for further plea and sentencing proceedings.

Another four Zimbabweans were arrested at a hotel in Johannesburg at the same time in a joint operation and are facing a different court process.

The investigation has involved South African police, Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies.

South Africa's Foreign Military Assistance Act was passed in 1998 at a time when the government was concerned about members of the former apartheid security services going to fight elsewhere in Africa.

There has been growing concern across Africa over the recruitment of its citizens to fight in the war in Ukraine, with some reportedly being lured to Russia by promises of lucrative civilian employment.

A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.

Some have been captured and are being held as prisoners of war.

In March, Kenya estimated that 252 of its citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia.

Kenyan Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue. He said an agreement had been reached for Russia to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.

In the same month, Zimbabwe said that 15 of its nationals had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia in Ukraine, with more than 60 still trapped on the frontlines.

The previous month, South Africa secured the return of 17 of its nationals who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.

In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.

South Africa's government said it condemned "the exploitation of young vulnerable people by individuals working with foreign military entities".

Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.

As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.

Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.

The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face the charge of "criminal conspiracy to commit fraud as part of an organised group and receiving stolen goods related to witness tampering". They deny any wrongdoing.

Umar Farouk Umar has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother, who reigned for 41 years

One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.

After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.

According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.

The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.

It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.

However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.

The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

KIGALI – Eighteen of Rwanda’s 27 districts have elected new mayors, while nine outgoing leaders have secured another five-year term, marking a significant turnover in district leadership following the November 24 elections.

The new leadership comprise 19 men and eight women, meaning women account for 29.63 per cent of the elected mayors, compared with 70.37 per cent for men.

The eight districts under women leadership are Musanze, Ngoma, Nyabihu, Gakenke, Kamonyi, Rwamagana, Rulindo and Ruhango. Six of the eight women are taking up the mayoral positions for the first time, while Vestine Mukandayisenga of Gakenke and Nathalie Niyonagira of Ngoma have retained their positions.

The figures also show that most districts will have new leadership, with only one in three outgoing mayors returning to office.

The other returning mayors are Gerald Muzungu of Karongi, Narcisse Mupenzi of Nyamasheke, Phanuel Sindayiheba of Rusizi, Fred Hategekimana of Kayonza, Prosper Mulindwa of Rubavu, Bruno Rangira of Kirehe and Henry Kakooza of Nyagatare.

Their return follows their election to the new district councils, which gave them the opportunity to seek another term as members of the district executive committees.

The remaining 18 districts have new mayors, including Musanze, where Marie-Grâce Berwa takes over, and Huye, where Vedaste Nshimiyimana has been elected.

Other new leaders include Jean-Léonard Sekanyange in Gatsibo, Ildephonse Niyibizi in Burera, Pierre Celestin Bimenyimana in Nyanza, Patricia Murekatete in Kamonyi and Sandra Musabwasoni in Rwamagana.

Some of the new mayors are not newcomers to local administration. Thaddée Habimana, elected in Nyamagabe, previously served as the district’s Vice Mayor in charge of economic development.

Women will lead eight of the 27 districts, with six new female mayors joining the two who retained their positions.

The newly elected women are Marie-Grâce Berwa in Musanze, Jacqueline Uwingabire in Nyabihu, Patricia Murekatete in Kamonyi, Sandra Musabwasoni in Rwamagana, Chantal Uwamahoro in Rulindo and Virginie Mukasonga in Ruhango.

Their representation comes after the election of women councilors earlier in the local government electoral process.

Each district council has 17 members, including five women representatives elected to meet the constitutional requirement for at least 30 per cent women’s representation in district councils.

However, the proportion of women among the mayors is slightly below that threshold, at 29.63 per cent.

Unlike elections in which residents directly vote for their district leaders, the mayors and their two deputies are selected by district councils through an indirect, secret-ballot process.

The councils were constituted through elections held on November 17 for women representatives and November 21 for general councilors, alongside representatives of special-interest groups.

Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge districts were not included in the elections because they do not have independent district councils and operate under a different administrative arrangement within the City of Kigali.

The newly elected mayors and their executive committees will serve from 2026 to 2031, overseeing district development programs, budgets and service delivery. With 18 districts changing mayors, the new term begins with a substantial change of local leadership.

Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.

Here's what you need to know about the payment.

For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.

A typical yearly energy bill is forecast to jump by £276 in January , according to consultants Cornwall Insight.

And some more recent forecasts suggest a typical annual bill could rise by £400 or so to £2,100 in January.

Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.

Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.

As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in , external . If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.

If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.

The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

He urged the devolved governments to follow suit to "give people of all nations in the UK breathing space on their energy bills this winter".

The Welsh government has said that it will also make a £100 cost-of-living payment to all households in council tax bands A to D.

The Scottish government said it would "seek to replicate" the £100 energy payment.

Meanwhile, the Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into the bank account that you use to pay it, from the start of January.

Those who don't pay by direct debit will have the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.

The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.

Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.

However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.

Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way of giving them the payments.

This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.

The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

The government has said the support is to help households with the cost of energy.

But the money will appear directly in people's bank accounts. As such, people could choose to spend it on something else.

The chancellor said the money for the £100 cash payments is coming from a tax rise on banks.

The surcharge on banks' corporation tax will rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028.

Bayern Munich are only focused on getting Jamal Musiala back from injury and are not interested in the comments made regarding his contract, the club's sporting director Max Eberl insisted.

The 23-year-old collapsed twice in four days during pre-season and said he had been diagnosed with "easily treatable absence seizures, which are due to a neurological dysfunction".

Last week, players' union Fifpro said Bayern Munich's hierarchy "should know better" after the club's honorary president Uli Hoeness said the midfielder may never "regain the performance level he once had".

Describing the talks on Tuesday as "very, very constructive", Eberl said the focus was on Musiala's recovery from a recent injury.

"Today it was about just how we want to get Jamal back on the field, just like before his muscle injury in the international break," Eberl said.

"That's the only task FC Bayern has currently, to give Jamal this trust and not some topics about money or something."

The Bundesliga club's chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen questioned the lucrative contract extension the Germany international signed in 2025, running until 2030, if Musiala fails to get back to his best form, while his predecessor Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested the deal , external may need to be renegotiated.

Bayern manager Vincent Kompany said in September it wouldn't be "a big deal" if the seizures return.

Musiala, previously a regular starter and one of the best young talents in Europe, has played five times this season, scoring twice.

"Contracts are there to be respected," Fifpro said on Saturday. "An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."

Huawei has been guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US, AP reports.

In the two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Manchester United defender Leny Yoro (second left) is shown a red card by referee Sam Barrott at Anfield

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has questioned the competence of video assistant referee officials after defender Leny Yoro had his red card overturned by the Football Association.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday after bringing down Aleksander Isak just outside the United penalty area.

United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.

Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.

"I am very disappointed," the Argentine said. "This type of thing can never happen.

"We can accept the referee can make a mistake. But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? Are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play 11 by 11? No.

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?"

United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.

They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.

It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.

Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on 13 September was allowed to stand even though a clearly offside Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play.

There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.

Instead, he has doubled down on the call, saying: "I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball."

United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.

The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.

This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.

Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.

"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," said Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.

"We need to defend my players and my club, and that is to denounce it and to say, the decision wasn't good. And now, the three points, where are the three points?"

What referee's chief Webb said about the incident on the Mic'd Up programme.

"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.

"That was the referee's call made on the field, and then the VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn't.

"That if there was any doubt, then it was doubt.

"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. and

"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.

"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable. Certainly not clearly wrong."

The substance was released near the end of US rapper Don Toliver's gig at Co-op Live on Sunday

An "unknown substance" that prompted a mass evacuation at a rap concert may be linked to robberies and stolen jewellery at the venue, police have said.

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One person was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said officers received nine reports of jewellery being stolen during the concert but no arrests had been made and the substance had not yet been identified.

The police scene has now been lifted at Co-op Live

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said there was "no wider ongoing risk" to the public.

"We are aware similar robberies have been reported at two European concerts for the same artist and will be linking in with our European counterparts to better understand the wider picture of this suspected offending," he said.

The substance was released at around 22:00 GMT, near the end of Toliver's show as part of his Nitrous – Octane world tour.

Afterwards, 88 people underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were accommodated at the neighbouring Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed.

Many were advised to seal their clothes in a bag overnight.

Friends Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing say they felt "unsafe" as they left the arena

Poppy Rutter and Sophie Billing, both 19, who had travelled from Cambridge to see the concert, said it was not immediately clear what had happened.

Sophie said: "I thought something had gone wrong with smoke coming off stage.

"We started to suffer, coughing and spluttering and feeling tight-chested. A member of staff said it was tear gas.

"Security rushed in and went straight to the pit. We only left as we were starting to feel unsafe and not 100 per cent well."

She said there was "no communication", adding: "You would think Manchester would be extra vigilant, given what's happened in the past."

Posting on Instagram on Monday, Toliver said: "I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night at Co-op Live.

"The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans."

He also asked that people stop bringing substances into his shows.

GMP urged anyone who feels unwell or develops symptoms following the concert to seek medical advice.

Sabrina Bahsoon now has more than 900,000 followers across social media

Sabrina Bahsoon became known globally as Tube Girl after self-shot videos of her dancing and lip-syncing on the London Underground blew up online.

The 26-year-old content creator had the world at her feet when she went viral in 2023 , going on to build a social media following of more than 900,000 people.

She signed major brand endorsement deals and was pursuing a music career.

But then her "whole life turned upside down" when she had what appeared to be a psychotic episode.

Her symptoms made her violent and erratic, leading to her being sectioned in a mental health hospital - where doctors treated her with anti-psychotic medication.

But Bahsoon's family, helped by her father's neurologist friend, pushed for further tests.

And two months into her hospital treatment, doctors got to the truth.

Sabrina Bahsoon shot to fame for her viral Tube videos but in March 2026 her life turned upside down overnight.

She actually had a rare, but treatable, autoimmune disease which is known to sometimes present as psychiatric symptoms, as well as seizures, confusion and memory loss.

In her first interview since the experience, she tells BBC News she wants hospitals to offer a series of tests as standard practice if patients have these symptoms.

"In a way I do feel let down by the care I received. I feel like the urgency to discover what was actually wrong with me wasn't there," she says.

"And I also feel as a woman being written off completely as a psychotic patient without further investigation was a mistake."

A spokesperson for the hospital she attended has apologised for Bahsoon's experience and says an investigation has been launched into her care.

The content creator was in hospital for about four months earlier this year

Bahsoon first had "psychotic symptoms" in March this year after filming a video on the Tube with girl group Flo.

She says that evening she began to scream, cry and her conversations became "very erratic".

The next day she broke up with her boyfriend, which prompted her sisters to check on her, as it was so unexpected.

Bahsoon says her condition got worse, becoming violent towards herself and posting videos which didn't make sense, before her sisters called 999 for an ambulance.

"I'm normally a very relaxed person, maybe anxious at times, but the way I was speaking about harming myself and the way I was screaming and being violent was super out of character for me," she says.

A&E doctors initially thought her symptoms could have been provoked by stress and a lack of sleep, discharging her with sleeping tablets.

She then began destroying things at home and spoke about having hallucinations, which led to police bringing her to hospital in handcuffs.

Bahsoon was sectioned and moved to a psychiatric ward where she was treated with antipsychotic medication, which she says made her "docile".

"I went from being a total firecracker to being completely catatonic," she says.

"I stopped eating, drinking. I could not speak properly."

Bahsoon has "very faint memories" of this period, she says, but her family has since shown her clips of her having breakdowns which she finds "heartbreaking".

Sabrina Bahsoon was pursuing a music career at the height of her fame

After two months on the psychiatric ward, Bahsoon was diagnosed with an autoimmune disease called anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

It was caused by tumours in her ovaries, known as teratomas, producing antibodies which attacked her body.

She had surgery to remove the tumours in June, which she says brought on a "drastic" change in her behaviour from "freaking out" to having more understanding of what was happening around her.

Bahsoon has since been recovering back in her home country of Malaysia and is having therapy to "deal with all the trauma".

But she says she feels "very lucky" as doctors have told her she is part of a small percentage of people who they expect to make a full recovery.

The content creator first revealed what happened in a TikTok video in October, and says she is sharing her story as she wants to raise awareness of the disease.

She also wants to "push people to advocate for themselves" if they feel they're not getting the "treatment they deserve".

"I do want reform in the way that hospitals deal with psychotic patients or patients that present with psychotic symptoms," she says.

"I hope I'm sharing my story so that nobody else has to go through this."

She plans to return to her content creation in the new year and is looking forward to "enjoying life with a whole new perspective and appreciation for what I do and what I now can help people with".

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is more typical in women and mainly affects young people, with about 40% of cases aged under 18, according to the charity Encephalitis International (EI) , external .

Dr Ava Easton MBE, chief executive of EI, says a "frightening" aspect is how quickly someone's behaviour and personality can appear to change.

"A person may suddenly seem confused, distressed or [to be] experiencing psychosis when the underlying problem is actually inflammation of their brain," she says.

She says there's a "real risk" of it going undiagnosed and encourages people to look out for the warning signs , external .

According to the NHS , external , cases of all types of encephalitis are rare, and EI says the condition affects about 6,000 people in the UK each year.

A spokesperson for Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, which was the first to treat Bahsoon, said they were "very sorry" for what she experienced.

They said an internal review found some aspects of her initial assessment "were not followed up as they should have been" and an investigation had been started.

Dr Ed Beveridge, divisional medical director at Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust, also confirmed they'd be part of that review.

He said anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis was a "rare autoimmune condition" that is not "routinely screened for nationally".

"We are pleased that her condition has now been identified and treated."

John Swinney has asked the government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled

At its heart this is a story about trust.

Trust in doctors and other health professionals at NHS Grampian to provide the highest standards of treatment and care.

Trust in their managers to effectively deal with problems when they arise.

And trust in the Scottish government to step in if that does not happen.

What we have learned about the operation of NHS Grampian in the last two weeks raises huge questions in all of these areas.

First we had a scathing report by the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland, which found serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership and oversight of clinical governance.

There was particular concern about patterns of repeated and avoidable harm, and the board's ability to learn from serious adverse events.

Does Scotland's NHS have a revolving door problem with senior managers?

Surgeon calls for corporate homicide probe over claims patients unnecessarily bled to death

Man who nearly died during liver surgery at Aberdeen hospital says mistakes were made

The Scottish government has sent in a support team to help the current management at NHS Grampian make improvements.

Questions have been raised about the suitability of some of those appointed to carry out this work given problems they have faced in their own areas of responsibility .

The watchdog's report was followed by a powerful intervention from a surgeon-turned-whistleblower who works at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

Dr Mohammed Habib said he had been raising serious concerns about liver and pancreatic services at the hospital for 10 years.

He released a previously unpublished review from 2022 that looked at 45 patients in the care of this specialist unit over the previous seven years.

It said that 31 had died, and 19 of them were considered to have died of avoidable consequences of surgery or intervention.

Nineteen people died and their deaths were potentially avoidable.

This finding was not made public by NHS Grampian or those in the Scottish government who knew about it.

This is where this story becomes political - because Dr Habib tried to get the attention of ministers.

He raised his concerns with the Scottish government including, he said, writing to the first minister on three occasions.

At Holyrood question time, John Swinney acknowledged that the issues raised were of the "gravest concern".

He said Dr Habib's messages had received "appropriate responses" from officials.

It seems they directed him to a national whistleblowing service and to the police.

Dr Habib said he wrote to the first minister on three occasions

This is what, in my view, makes this potentially the most dangerous political moment for John Swinney since he took over as first minister in 2024.

A surgeon writes to him because 19 people may have died unnecessarily as a result of how they were treated by the NHS and nothing seems to happen.

We have since been told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of this correspondence.

That in turn raises questions about the operation of the highest political office in devolved Scotland.

After two decades in power would the SNP administration not have an established system for deciding what should and should not be seen by the first minister?

And if a pattern of seemingly avoidable deaths in the NHS is not serious enough to be escalated to the top then what is?

Swinney seemed to recognise the inadequacy of his parliamentary answers fairly quickly.

Soon after question time his team said he had asked the Scottish government's top civil servant to review how correspondence is handled.

This too was only the beginning of a realisation within government that this had the potential to develop into a political disaster.

By Saturday, Health Secretary Angela Constance had decided to announce an independent review into who knew what and when, what they did with the information - and why.

Before the weekend was out, she was on BBC Scotland's The Sunday Show promising 100% transparency and accountability.

She seemed angry to have been left carrying the can for something that should have been dealt with more robustly at a far earlier stage.

Angela Constance said the inquiry's findings would be published in full

We have now learned that the review will be led by an experienced King's Counsel , and the likelihood is that they will come from outside Scotland.

Constance has said that any clinical input they receive will definitely come from outside Scotland.

The KC will be able to scrutinise the actions of current and former ministers, civil servants, and those working in the health service.

Constance said their findings would be published in full and that any urgent matters that arise during the review should be reported directly to relevant bodies.

The minister also said it was "categorically false" to say that no action was taken following the 2022 report, which was drawn up by University of Edinburgh Professor Stephen Wigmore.

Constance said liver and pancreatic surgery was suspended for a time, then resumed under the professor's supervision until he was satisfied it could continue without his oversight.

It was stopped again on at least two further occasions and patients requiring complex surgery have been transferred to NHS Lothian since early this year.

It has been reported that former Health Secretary Humza Yousaf and current chief medical officer Sir Gregor Smith were aware of the 2022 review.

Yousaf has made clear he supports full scrutiny and "further dramatic action" in NHS Grampian. Sir Gregor has yet to make any public comment.

The review process will not necessarily contain this crisis of confidence.

More patients and their families may come forward to share their experiences, or perhaps others within NHS Grampian will choose to speak out.

The involvement of the campaigning lawyer Aamer Anwar, who is working with Dr Habib, increases the likelihood of this type of follow-up.

There will undoubtedly be further parliamentary scrutiny, with the possibility of key figures being called before a Holyrood committee.

It is worth remembering that the police are also taking an interest and have yet to determine whether or not a formal investigation is merited.

Some have hinted at the potential need for a judge-led public inquiry, although these tend to take a very long time and cost a huge amount of money.

There are already three health-related public inquiries into Covid handling, major hospital building projects in Glasgow and Edinburgh, and botched brain surgery in Dundee.

The deaths of 19 people at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary could have been avoided

There is a clear determination by government and opposition at Holyrood to see a much faster remedy to the complexity of problems in NHS Grampian.

A turnaround in healthcare delivery and management in north east Scotland is being pursued alongside radical plans to overhaul how the NHS is run across the country.

The government is proposing to merge the existing network of regional health boards into just two for the whole of mainland Scotland.

There will be those who argue that this provides an opportunity to create a more robust system of supervision and a more rapid response when things go wrong.

Others fear that this kind of centralisation could result in local deficiencies being overlooked.

This could become an important feature in the debate over NHS reform.

In the meantime, the Scottish government has to convince the public and political rivals that it has got a grip of what's happening in NHS Grampian.

That seems essential if patients are to have confidence that they can place their trust in the vital services it provides.

Moyin Odeniran said he was "in shock" after being crowned the winner of the 17th series of The Great British Bake Off.

"He has done an amazing job because out of all the bakers he struggled at the beginning, and he actually got better and better," Hollywood said.

Fellow judge Nigella Lawson praised Odeniran as a "worthy winner", but also said the other finalists were "sensational".

Odeniran said he would never forget his time on the show

Reflecting on his performance in the final, Odeniran said: "I didn't want to put too much pressure on myself, but I knew I had put my best foot forward.

"I couldn't have done anything better than I did and I had a great time doing it."

He said he got "quite exhausted" while filming the series and praised his mother, sister and close friends for their support.

"Earlier on, some of the challenges were quite difficult for me and I was shocked that I kept going through," Odeniran said.

"Before you get there you think you know how to bake, and by week two you question whether you know anything about baking."

British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study reveals.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' ( Natsal , external ) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

Half of people aged 16 to 24 have sent or received sexual images on their phone in the last year, while one in two young women and almost nine in 10 young men say they have viewed pornography.

But a third of this age group have never had sex, up from a fifth in the last study 12 years ago.

Adults under 45 are having less sex too, doing it twice a month, on average, down from once a week in 1990.

More than one in three (37%) women said they had watched porn in the past year.

For men, it was around four in every five (81%).

Among the 16-24 year-olds, half of women and most young men (86%) said they watched it.

Porn use and masturbation were less common among people who had never had sex, which the authors say suggests solo and online activity is not simply replacing in-person sex, although they cannot be sure.

They didn't ask about AI or virtual relationships with romantic chatbots, but say they probably should next time.

Soazig Clifton, one of the Natsal team and from University College London, said: "When we did our fieldwork in 2022-24 that seemed a little bit sci-fi.

"In the future we might be looking at the impact of AI on people's sexual behaviour and on their relationships, thinking about things like AI companions."

Co-researcher Prof Wendy Macdowall, from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), says while it may be tempting to blame screen time for less sex, it's likely many other factors are involved, "especially for young people."

Young people are drinking less alcohol than past generations and more live at home with their parents, for example.

Rising rates of mental health conditions might also be involved, along with the Covid pandemic that stopped people going out.

She says more open discussion of consent could also mean young people feel better able to decide whether and when to have sex.

But some are troubled by their sex lives.

One in seven women (14%) reported ongoing upset with others about things done to them in their sexual past.

The same proportion of men reported feeling shame about some of their sexual thoughts and desires.

This fourth Natsal survey reveals trends, but cannot fully explain them.

The previous one, in 2010, suggested having sex too soon was the biggest regret of young people losing their virginity.

Now, it appears more are waiting longer.

Almost two in five young women (38%) and more than one in four young men (28%) now report never having had sex. That is up from around one in five in the earlier surveys of 1990, 2000 and 2010.

And among all adults who are having sex, most are doing it less often. The average used to be once a week. Now, it's fortnightly.

The latest results, published in The Lancet and based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16-59 selected at random across Britain, reveal:

three-quarters of adults have had sex in the past year

the average number of sexual partners in a lifetime is five

women have sex once a month and men twice a month, on average

reports of sex with a same-sex partner have increased among both men and women, but by how much is less clear

Many Brits, young people in particular, are having unprotected sex that can lead to pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), the figures suggest.

And use of the oral contraceptive pill has declined among young women.

But more women now say they do not want children - a doubling in the past decade, from 8% to 17% among those aged 16–44.

"Understanding what's driving this – whether economic insecurity, climate anxiety or changing life priorities – should now be a priority for future research and policy, as it has real implications for planning health, care and family services," says researcher Dr Laura Oakley from the LSHTM.

Rayan Cherki (left) rescued a late draw for Manchester City against Napoli

Manchester City's slick footballing machine is starting to grind to a halt.

The quick passing patterns and edge-of-the-seat action that was evident for so long under former manager Pep Guardiola was supposed to be taken forward by incumbent Enzo Maresca.

It started flawlessly under the Italian with the side winning their first eight games, but that smooth operation is beginning to turn into a turgid and pedestrian showing.

Similar to Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham, moans and groans filled a rather flat Etihad Stadium as the home faithful watched their side labour to a 2-2 Champions League draw against Napoli.

City's recent defensive issues also continued, now conceding in 10 successive games and letting in the first goal in seven of those matches.

Maresca said: "We are always looking for three points but when you are not able to win it is important you that don't lose. We take the point, five games [played],10 points and overall I think it is a good result in the end.

"Today, off the ball, once again we didn't concede a lot, the problem is that in this moment they are clinical when we concede a chance, almost every time it is finishing with a goal. We created many chances but in this moment it is like this and move on.

"The first 10 games we always scored first and then in this moment it is exactly in the opposite way, we just need to find a way to avoid that, but I don't think it affects the players in terms of their confidence. We fought until the end."

Cherki rescues point for Man City against Napoli

City were strong favourites for this game and should have had few issues in collecting all three points against a Napoli side that are languishing in eighth place in Serie A.

Their injury issues mean they were able to name only seven substitutes, two of those being goalkeepers, while they had suffered defeat in their past three meetings with City.

They threatened a shock result after twice going ahead through well-taken goals from Rasmus Hojlund and Noa Lang, but Rayan Cherki managed to salvage a late draw for the hosts.

Maresca's side had 62.7% possession and attempted 665 passes, which largely lacked incisiveness, and of that figure 303 were in the final third compared to Napoli's 77.

The latest disappointing result means City's perfect start is quickly unravelling, now having won only one of their past seven games in all competitions inside 90 minutes.

"It was really surprising to see Manchester City so dull in the first half and so predictable," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"If you play a team that takes their time, you get yourself set. It is 100% easier to defend.

"You sit and watch City pass, pass, pass, slow, slow. You can get a cigar out."

Star striker Erling Haaland has been in prolific form again this season, scoring 20 goals for club and country, but the 26-year-old has drawn a blank in his past two games.

The Norwegian had chances but failed to score against Fulham on Saturday and though he was handed the captain's armband against Napoli, Haaland was on the periphery for much of the game.

The frontman managed only 14 touches of the ball against the Serie A side on Tuesday, the lowest figure of any player that started the match.

It raises the question whether he is receiving the service to try and find the back of the net.

"I feel I am getting more than enough chances to score," Haaland told TNT Sports. "We tried to push at the end for a goal but we couldn't. Not good enough and we let them in too easy.

"Football is easy and difficult; when you win it's easy and you know what to do, when you don't you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think but it's not so easy."

City are sixth in the Champions League table, before Wednesday's games, but in the Premier League they have failed to win their past four.

It does not get any easier this weekend, facing a daunting trip to leaders Arsenal on Sunday as they aim to find some form.

Haaland added: "It's the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away.

"We need a top performance from every single player."

Manager Jose Mourinho described Jude Bellingham as "without any doubt, the best midfielder in the world" following a wonder goal which inspired a brilliant second-half performance for Real Madrid in a 5-1 win against PSV .

Mourinho opted to leave the England midfielder out of the starting line-up for Tuesday's Champions League game at the Bernabeu - an understandable decision given the demands of Madrid's fixture schedule and the strength in depth at his disposal.

But after watching his side trail 1-0 at half-time against the Dutch side, Mourinho knew changes were needed.

"He is an amazing player that has everything," the Portuguese manager said. "He has physicality, he understands the game, he has absolutely everything. Today, he has changed how the game was evolving."

Captain Fede Valverde equalised in the 50th minute and 10 minutes later Bellingham produced his moment of magic.

Receiving the ball just outside the penalty area, he took two touches to lift it into position before unleashing a magnificent volley with the outside of his right footr, leaving PSV keeper Matej Kovar with no chance.

It was a sensational finish, executed with extraordinary precision.

"I was a bit surprised, honestly," Bellingham said about the goal. "I knew that I could control the ball well and get it into my grasp. But normally from there, I'm looking to see who's on as an option to play through.

"It popped up nicely and I thought I'm just going to hit it. So yeah, it was a nice goal and important for the team, being the second goal, and gave us control."

The 23-year-old celebrated in trademark fashion, standing with his arms outstretched in front of the home supporters as thousands serenaded him with chants of 'Hey Jude'.

It was his fourth goal in his past five appearances for Real.

Asked whether he should be compared to Real and France legend Zinedine Zidane, who won the Ballon d'Or and World Cup in 1998, Bellingham maintained his humility.

"I think Zidane is much better than me. He's much more elegant and he's my idol," he said.

Kylian Mbappe scored two more goals and Vinicius Junior put away the fifth to complete a super turnaround from a team that had looked short of ideas in the first half.

At the suggestion that he is currently in the form of his life, Bellingham said: "I think you're only as good as your next one [game]. Your last one doesn't really matter.

"But my focus has to change now to preparing for the next game. Thinking about my best form or being the best player in the world doesn't mean anything to me."

For Bellingham, the ability to respond when things are not going according to plan is what separates the best teams from the rest.

"We're managing to show that mentality that good teams do, that even if you're not playing well, you can raise the level at any point," he said.

His adaptation to life in Spain has also been an important part of that journey.

Asked about his increasingly impressive Spanish, Bellingham admitted he still gets nervous when speaking the language in public.

"It's getting a little bit better. I get a little bit nervous speaking to you guys. It's much easier in the changing room," he joked to journalists.

"I'm loving living in Spain. I'm loving the club. I think for English players it's such an important thing to go and move abroad and learn new things and I've obviously benefited massively from that."

And while his performances have inevitably brought renewed attention to individual awards, Bellingham said that personal recognition is not what motivates him.

Asked about the Ballon d'Or, he said his focus was only on the team.

"I don't care about the Ballon d'Or, honestly. I want to win a lot of titles with the team, the Champions League, the League."

"The Ballon d'Or is something for you, journalists, to vote and create a bit of tension. But for me it's more important that the team win."

It might be emerging more as a theme than as a major problem, but in recent weeks Arsenal cannot seem to finish off matches when they are on top.

In their past nine outings across all competitions, just once have the Gunners won a game by more than a single goal.

The latest frustration came in Tuesday's 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund, though perspective is needed. Arsenal might consider it as two points dropped having gone into half-time ahead, but they remain unbeaten in the current Champions League league phase and have not lost at this stage of the competition for more than two years.

But of late, despite dominating large parts of matches, Arsenal have had periods where they have dropped off and allowed opponents back into the game.

Against Slavia Prague away in the Champions League, after scoring twice in the first half, Arsenal 's standards dropped. The same happened against Newcastle in the Premier League last weekend where they found themselves 2-1 behind in the second half having led at the break, before recovering to eventually draw 2-2.

They are producing periods of high-level football, but the struggles to consistently turn that into more goals can lead to nervy finishes.

In the draw with Bundesliga leaders Dortmund, Arsenal had 30 shots but just four of those attempts were on target.

Boss Mikel Arteta mentioned the failure to capitalise post match, though was keen to praise his side's "brilliant performance".

"The way we played, bearing in mind the opposition that we played today and what we've done out there, is just something to be very, very pleased [about] because there is very little more that you can demand from the team," Arteta said.

"But obviously, the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance in the amount of chances (and) situations.

"There is an element of luck; there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist because I think what the team has done and shown today, I think it's the right direction."

Arsenal held by Borussia Dortmund in Champions League

Arteta made six changes to the side that drew with Newcastle , with one of the biggest calls to rest striker Kai Havertz and bring in Viktor Gyokeres.

The striker has had a difficult season so far, with four of his seven starts coming in the Champions League against opposition where Arsenal have been favourites.

However, Gyokeres scored a powerful effort from outside the area to give Arsenal the lead against Dortmund.

Overall though, it ended up being a mixed night for the 28-year-old as he missed a header from inside the six-yard-box that would have surely won the game for the Gunners late on.

Arteta was asked if the chances his side are missing were down to mentality, misfortune or composure.

"There is an element of luck here because how some of the goals they haven't gone inside, I don't know.

"The execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think it was really, really good."

Arteta was also full of praise for Gyokeres, with particular emphasis on the striker's link-up play; an element of his game at times criticised.

"What I love the most is how connected he was to the team," Arteta said.

"We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threaded in behind and stretched the pitch.

"There was a lot to like in that performance and that's the Viktor that we needed."

Noni Madueke has been Arsenal 's best attacker in recent weeks.

The winger, who was left out of the last England squad, is enjoying a run in the Arsenal starting XI with Bukayo Saka out injured and is taking his opportunity.

Madueke has registered a goal and two assists in his past three games and was again the best Arsenal forward against Dortmund.

The Gunners host Manchester City on Sunday and are currently six points clear at the top of the Premier League table.

Madueke, who was frustrated with the performance against Dortmund, said the clash with third-placed City is a great chance to get back to winning ways and shake off any frustration.

"I think these are the best games. I'm really looking forward to it. Two draws on the bounce now and I just desperately want to win on the weekend and I know my team-mates feel the same," Madueke told Amazon Prime.

"We are going to do everything we have to win the three points. We're champions, we're at home. We have a duty to perform well at the Emirates.

"There are things we need to improve but all in all we are going in the right direction."
